tutorial.seoTitle: React Performance Tutorial: memo, useMemo and useCallback

chapters.title: Measure Before Optimising

chapters.description: How React.memo works, and the reason it so often does nothing.

questions.question: What should you do before adding memoisation?
options: Wrap every component in memo as a precaution
Measure with the Profiler and browser performance tools to find the real bottleneck
questions.explanation: Most components are already fast. Without measurement you are likely to add cost and complexity where there was no problem.

questions.question: What does React.memo compare?
questions.explanation: It is a shallow prop comparison. Objects, arrays and functions compare by reference, which is why unstable props defeat it.

questions.question: Why does memo do nothing for this child?
options: memo only works on class components
Both props are created fresh on every parent render, so they never compare equal
memo requires a custom comparison function
questions.explanation: The filtered array and the inline arrow function are new references each render. Stabilise them with useMemo and useCallback, or the memo is pure overhead.

questions.question: What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback?
options: useMemo is for effects, useCallback is for events
useMemo caches a computed value, useCallback caches a function
questions.explanation: `useCallback(fn, deps)` is exactly `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`. One caches the result of a calculation, the other caches the function itself.

questions.question: When is useMemo worth adding?
options: Around every calculation in a component
When the calculation is genuinely expensive, or the identity of the result matters to a memoised child or an effect
Whenever a component has more than three props
questions.explanation: Those are the two payoffs. Elsewhere it adds a dependency array to maintain and a comparison on every render for no gain.

questions.question: Which approach avoids re-rendering an expensive subtree without any memoisation?
options: Passing it as children so it is created by a component that does not re-render
questions.explanation: Content passed as children is created by the outer component, so state changes in the middle component do not recreate it.

questions.question: What does list virtualisation do?
options: Renders only the rows currently visible plus a small buffer
Moves rendering to a web worker
questions.explanation: Keeping the DOM small is what makes very long lists scroll smoothly - the benefit grows with the size of the data.

questions.question: Where does code splitting give the biggest win?
options: At route boundaries and around heavy dependencies such as chart or editor libraries
questions.explanation: Routes and large libraries are big enough that the saved bytes outweigh the extra request. Splitting tiny components costs more than it saves.
